notorious

/noh-TOR-ee-us/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Notorious means widely known for something bad — famous for a negative quality or deed.

The old harbor town was once notorious for smugglers who slipped past the dock inspectors every night.

Example

That airline is notorious for losing checked luggage, so Maya packs everything she truly needs into her carry-on.

The airline is famous specifically for a bad practice — that negative fame is what notorious means, and it explains why Maya takes precautions.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disreputable: Disreputable means widely distrusted — the word for a business, district, or character that respectable people avoid because it seems dishonest or seedy. Notorious is about fame rather than trust: a notorious place is famous for something bad, and everyone, respectable or not, has heard of it.

ill-famed: Ill-famed says exactly what it sounds like: carrying a bad name. It is the quieter, more literary twin of notorious, and it stops at the reputation itself. Notorious adds active celebrity — the bad name is widely circulated, traded in stories, known far beyond its home.

scandalous: Scandalous describes behavior that shocks propriety — affairs, frauds, outrages that set tongues wagging. Notorious describes the resulting fame: after enough scandalous conduct, a person becomes notorious. The behavior is scandalous; the reputation it earns is notorious.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

reputable: widely trusted and well regarded

esteemed: held in high regard

Where it sits · how fiercely the public turns against it

unpopular → notorious → reviled

unpopular vs. notorious: An unpopular policy is disliked, but a notorious one is famous specifically for being bad.

reviled vs. notorious: Reviled is stronger than notorious — the person or thing is not just known for bad qualities but actively hated.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — not-: known (Latin notus, from noscere, 'to come to know')

Suffix — -orious: full of; characterized by

Put it together: Notorious comes from Latin notus, 'known' — literally 'fully known.' Over the centuries the word narrowed, so that today this fame is always for something bad.

Use the root in a new word: notable: Her free-throw percentage showed a notable improvement after a summer of daily practice.

Root Check

Word Choice

Common / journalistic

Notorious always carries negative fame — a notorious outlaw, a road notorious for accidents. Don't use it for positive fame; that's renowned or celebrated. Its related noun form, infamy, names the state of having that bad reputation.
